keywords_required:
The number of live births per 1000 people per year.
[1 mark]

The highest birth rates (over 30.01 per thousand) are mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa [1].
An exception is Afghanistan [1]. The lowest levels (less than 10 per thousand) are
found in Russia, China and Eastern and Southern Europe [1]. Relatively high rates
(20.01–30 per thousand) are found in other parts of Africa and parts of the Middle
East [1], whereas much of North America, Western Europe and the Middle East have
relatively low rates [1].
[Max 3 marks]

High birth rates are mainly found in populations with a youthful age structure [1],
in rural households [1] where children may be seen as an asset to work on the land [1],
and/or where there is limited access to family planning measures/contraceptives [1].
[Max 3 marks]

The number of deaths per 1000 people per year.
[1 mark]

The highest death rates (12 per thousand and over) are found in Russia and Eastern
Europe [1]. Afghanistan is an exception [1]. The lowest death rates are found in North

Africa and the Middle East [1], parts of East Africa and West Africa [1], and parts of
Central and South America [1].
[Max 3 marks]

One major reason for high death rates is the number/percentage of elderly people in a
population [1]. As a population ages, the death rate increases [1]. Countries with youthful
age structures generally have lower death rates, such as many parts of North and East
Africa [1]. Afghanistan is an exception – the high death rate there is likely to be due
directly/indirectly to conflict [1]. The Central African Republic also has a high death rate,
and this may be due to poverty and the spread of infectious disease [1].       [Max 3 marks]

The proportion of young people, adults and elderly in a population.
[1 mark]

Most rural migrants are young adults [1], so when they leave a rural area the
population age structure becomes more elderly [1]. In contrast, as those migrants
move to urban areas, those areas show a higher proportion of young adults [1]. Younger
adults may lead to an increase in the birth rate, making the urban age structure even
younger [1].
[Max 3 marks]

There are many advantages and disadvantages of ageing populations. Much will depend on
the health and age of the people concerned. Disadvantages are likely to include the cost of
health care, pensions (in some countries), subsidised transport and a declining workforce.
Advantages can include the size of the ‘grey market’, the skills/knowledge that many elderly
people have, the care provided by elderly people for the young. The age of the elderly is a
factor – those aged 65–75 years may provide more benefits whereas those aged over 85 years
may be more in need of support. Answers should refer to places (countries/areas within a
country) with a large proportion of elderly people. Do not award more than 5 marks in the
following instances: if the answer only includes advantages or disadvantages; if the answer
does not include any named areas; if the answer has no evaluation.     [Max 7 marks]
